deep.reconstruction:
This is not a computation page. It is a prose draft of the opening of Riemann's Göttingen doctoral dissertation, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse' (1851). The wording of Art. 1 is almost identical to the printed text.

Art. 1 (as finally intended, after deletions). If z is a variable quantity that can successively take all possible real values, and to each of its values there corresponds a single value of the undetermined quantity w, then w is called a function of z. If, while z runs continuously through all values lying between two fixed values, w also changes continuously, the function is called continuous (stetig oder continuirlich) within this interval. This definition clearly establishes no law at all between the individual values of the function. Once the function has been specified on a given interval, the manner of its continuation outside that interval remains entirely arbitrary.

In modern terms: a function is an arbitrary single-valued assignment f: I ⊂ R → R (the Dirichlet-style definition). Continuity on an interval is described informally: w varies continuously as z varies continuously. The point being made is that values on one interval do not determine the extension, in contrast with the analytic functions treated later in the dissertation.

Art. 2 (entirely struck out here). The draft begins to contrast this with dependence given by a mathematical law, 'so dass durch bestimmte mathematische Operationen zu einem jeden Werthe von z der ihm entsprechende w gefunden wird'. A deleted parenthesis refers to 'functionis continuae nach Euler'schem Begriff' (my reading of this phrase is tentative), i.e. Euler's 'functio continua', meaning a function given by a single analytic expression. The printed Art. 2 keeps the 'mathematisches Gesetz' contrast. I am not certain whether it keeps the Euler reference.

Marginalia and scratch work:
(a) Left margin: pencil sketches of closed curves, including figure-eight and nested, self-overlapping loops. These are plausibly connected with the dissertation's discussion of closed boundary curves and multiply covered regions. This is my interpretation.
(b) Bottom of the page: crossed-out formula fragments, apparently written upside down. They seem to involve the differential dz/(1-z^2), an integral sign, and expressions like ∂θ/∂θ. They are too fragmentary to reconstruct a derivation. The integral ∫dz/(1-z^2) = (1/2)log((1+z)/(1-z)) may be the object, but that is my conjecture.
errors: No mathematical errors can be assessed. The text is a definition. In modern terms the continuity notion is informal, with no epsilon-delta formulation, but this is standard for 1851 and matches the printed dissertation.
The bottom formula fragments are illegible or struck out. No derivation can be checked.

results.what: General (arbitrary-correspondence) definition of a function of a real variable, with the remark that values on one interval impose no law on the continuation outside it
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet (1837), with antecedents in Euler (1755), Fourier and Lobachevsky; Riemann's dissertation Art. 1 (1851) is a well-known adoption

results.what: Informal definition of continuity on an interval
Deleted contrast with Euler's 'functio continua' (function given by one analytic law)
results.modern_name: Euler's distinction between continuous and discontinuous (mixed) functions

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the well-known first articles of Riemann's 1851 dissertation, nearly verbatim. The only mildly interesting details are the deletions, such as the struck reference to the Euler-style functio continua, and the curve sketches. These matter for genetic or editorial history but add no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: Speculative reading of the bottom fragment: an antiderivative of 1/(1-z^2) is (1/2)log((1+z)/(1-z)), i.e. atanh(z) (result should be 0).
atanh(z) is an antiderivative of 1/(1-z^2) (result should be 0).

transcription_corrections: Line 2: Riemann writes 'wird' above the line, replacing 'heisst'. The intended sentence is 'so wird, wenn jedem ihrer Werthe ein einziger ... Werth der unbestimmten Grösse w entspricht, w eine Function von z genannt', matching the printed dissertation. The transcription's '{+so+} heisst' should be read accordingly.
'zwischen zwei festen Werthen gelegenen Werthe' is correct. The deleted 'Werthe' precedes it after 'alle'.
The struck parenthesis in Art. 2 is better read as '(functionis continuae nach Euler'schem Begriff)' or similar, a reference to Euler's notion. 'Begriff' remains uncertain.
The bottom formula fragments appear to be written upside down relative to the text and are mostly struck out. The machine transcription's formulas there ('z/√z', '∂θ/∂θ') are unreliable.
The marginal drawings on the left (figure-eight and nested loop curves) are not transcribed. They should be noted as figures.
